title: Stark DD calls special meeting to rescind levy request, consider new one - NewsBreak
text: PLAIN TWP − The head of the Stark County Board of Developmental Disabilities has called a special meeting to rescind the board's passage of a request for a 2.65-mill replacement levy and consider requesting a different levy. A meeting notice issued at 7:35 p.m. July 30 said the Stark DD board would meet in a special meeting at 6 p.m. July 31 at Stark DD's Whipple-dale Center offices. The meeting notice does not give the reason why Stark DD would rescind its levy request from July 29 . But it may have to do with the fact the Ohio House July 21 voted to override Gov. Mike DeWine's veto of legislation that would eliminate replacement levies. And the Senate may also override the veto. William Green, Stark DD's superintendent could not be immediately reached for comment on July 30. Stark DD's director of communications, Lisa Parramore, said she did not have any additional information as to the reason for the meeting. Related: Ohio House overrides DeWine veto on property tax levies, tables other votes State law requires a special meeting notice be sent out to the media 24 hours before the meeting, meaning the latest notice may not meet that requirement. Parramore said she got the request by Green to send out the meeting notice around 6 p.m. July 30. And she needed time to write the notice and email it by 7:35 p.m. On July 29, the Stark DD board passed a declaration of necessity for a 2.65-mill permanent replacement levy that would replace three existing continuing levies from the 1980s. The Stark Commissiones voted July 30 to ask the Stark County Auditor's office to certify how much such a new levy would raise, which must be done before the levy can be placed on the ballot. The commissioners have to vote to place a Stark DD on the ballot before the state election filing deadline of 4 p.m. Aug. 6. Green told the board that due to costs rising faster than anticipated, Stark DD needed a new levy starting next year to avoid going $13.3 million into the red by 2028. If the replacement levy had been approved by voters, it would cost property owners about $70 more per year per $100,000 in valuation of their property and raise an additional $21.5 million a year. (This story will be updated as more information becomes available.)
